Chasles proved that if an ellipse be intersected in the point <math>\text{A}</math> by a confocal hyperbola, and from any point <math>\text{P}</math> on the hyperbola tangents <math>\text{PT}</math>, <math>\text{PT}'</math> be drawn to the ellipse, then the difference of the arcs of the ellipse <math>\text{TA}</math>, <math>\text{T}'\text{A}</math> = the difference of the tangents <math>\text{PT}</math>, <math>\text{PT}'</math>; and subsequently Graves showed that if from any point <math>\text{P}</math> on the outer of two confocal ellipses tangents be drawn to the inner, then the excess of the sum of the tangents <math>\text{PT}</math>, <math>\text{PT}'</math> over the intercepted arc <math>\text{TT}'</math> is constant. Precisely the same theorems hold for a quadric replacing the confocals by lines of curvature and the rectilineal tangents by geodetic tangents. Hart still further developed the analogies with confocal conics, and established the following : If a geodetic polygon circumscribe a line of curvature, and all its vertices but one move on lines of curvature, this vertex will also describe a line of curvature, and when the lines of curvature all belong to the same system the perimeter of the polygon will be constant.

2. ''Geodetics on Developable Surfaces.''—On these the geodetics are the curves which become right lines when the surface is unrolled into a plane. From this property a first integral can be immediately deduced.

3. ''Geodetics on Surfaces of Revolution.''—In all such the geodetics are the curves given by the equation <math>r \sin \phi = \text{const}</math>, <math>r</math> being the perpendicular on the axis of revolution, <math>\phi</math> the angle at which the curve crosses the meridian.
readings.c1s2:
¶
The general problem of the determination of geodetics on any surface may be advantageously treated in connexion with that of “parallel” curves. By “parallel” curves are meant curves whose geodetic distances from one another are constant—in other words, the orthogonal trajectories of a system of geodetics. In applying this method the determination of a system of parallel curves comes first, and the determination of the geodetics to which they are orthogonal follows as a deduction. If <math>\phi\ (u, v) = \text{const}</math> be a system of parallel curves, it is shown that <math>\phi</math> must satisfy the partial differential equation
{{block center|<math>\text{E} \left(\frac{d\phi}{dv}\right)^2 - 2\text{F} \left(\frac{d\phi}{du}\right) \left(\frac{d\phi}{dv}\right) + \text{G} \left(\frac{d\phi}{dv}\right)^2 = \text{EG} - \text{F}^2.</math>}}

If <math>\phi\ (u, v, a) = \text{const}</math> be a system of parallel curves satisfying this equation, then <math>d\phi/da = \text{const}</math> is proved to represent the orthogonal geodetics. The same method enables us to establish a result first arrived at by Jacobi, that whenever a first integral of the differential equation for geodetics can be found, the final integral is always reducible to quadratures. In this method <math>\phi</math> corresponds to the characteristic function in the Hamiltonian dynamics, the geodetics being the paths of a particle confined to the surface when no extraneous forces are in action.
